name: Marco Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so please tell me both what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Marco, 43, and a junior developer at a tech company after a two-year college diploma. I check payroll exports against timesheets and help fix the rules that turn hours into pay slips; I like when every shift can be accounted for. I am still learning the harder rules, and I don't use AI tools. My partner's flower stall and our two school-age children make Thursday pay checks feel rather less abstract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a small sorting program is fine if I can still see every payroll exception. I don't use AI tools myself; when a pay slip is wrong, I want the original hours and the rule in front of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my junior job can continue if the tools stay small. My pay is normal for this work, we have about two months of expenses saved, and a few software firms are within a long bus ride. My partner sells flowers at a market, which helps with school costs but changes with the season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking payroll exports against the timesheets each Thursday and ask the senior developer to show me the tax-code cases I still get wrong. In the first year we'd keep our present mortgage payment and save 50 from my pay each month if the market stall brings enough for school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than frightened. My wage covers the mortgage now, but two months saved is not much if either of us has a bad season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Whose pay slip showed you a problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cleaner once showed me a pay slip missing Sunday hours. The export file looked neat, but the paper rota told a different story. I had to ask the senior developer how to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How reliable is the flower stall income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flower stall does well before holidays and less well in wet weeks. If sales fall, we skip the 50 transfer; we do not pretend the market owes us a steady wage.

say: I'd accept **exception sorting** only if every pay slip can still be checked.
I'd say **paper rotas** can reveal hours missing from an export.
think: I expect my **junior payroll work** to continue if AI stays small.
I worry about **seasonal flower sales** and only two months saved.
do: Keep checking **Thursday payroll exports** against timesheets.
Ask a **senior developer** to explain the tax-code cases I miss.
Save **50 monthly** only if flower sales cover school costs.
feel: **Uneasy** about the cushion and seasonal sales, with work steady.
S0.quote: The export file looked neat, but the paper rota told a different story.
fieldNote: **Two months saved** and seasonal stall sales keep a background worry even when AI changes little.
He avoids AI tools and trusts a **timesheet trail** after finding a cleaner's missing Sunday hours.

steps.text: Check Thursday payroll exports against timesheets and ask about hard tax codes
Save 50 monthly only if flower sales cover school costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say writing pay rules, checking exports and answering employers are much of our work, so management should name the tasks AI will take. I don't want a faster payroll file if the Sunday hours vanish again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our firm might keep the senior developer to check AI-made rules and drop one of the juniors. I could be that person; two months saved and a long bus ride to the next software firm leave little margin, even if the flower stall stays open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager for a list of payroll checks people will still sign and keep my own record of every mismatch I can explain. In the first year, only if the firm proves AI catches missing hours and introduces it on exports, I'd learn on old files with a colleague, then compare one pay cycle with paper rotas; I'd defer replacing our old car while staffing is unclear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I am slow with new tools, but I know what a missing Sunday shift does to a family budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What spending decision could wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car is old but gets us to the market and school. A newer one would mean a loan, so we can postpone that decision while the firm changes its staffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the tool after seeing a tested process?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If management shows a tested process that catches the missing-hour cases, I could learn to check its output with a colleague. I would start with copies of old files, not this week's wages.

say: I'd ask which **human payroll checks** remain after AI takes routine work.
I'd insist on testing **missing Sunday hours** before removing manual review.
think: I could lose **my junior post** if a senior checks AI-made rules.
I have **two months saved** and only some nearby jobs, so a search would be tight.
do: Record **payroll mismatches** and ask my manager who signs future checks.
Learn **AI export checks** with a colleague on old files only after a tested process catches missing hours.
Delay an **old-car replacement** while staffing is unclear.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible cut and the long job search.
S1.quote: I am slow with new tools, but I know what a missing Sunday shift does to a family budget.
fieldNote: **High thinking exposure** puts junior payroll rules and checks at risk even without robot changes.
He is willing to **inspect AI output** only after a tested process and with old files under a colleague's guidance.

steps.text: Keep recording payroll mismatches and ask manager about future human sign-off
Learn AI export checks on old files with colleague only after process catches missing hours
Delay replacing old family car while software staffing remains unclear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI by 2028 would write and check payroll rules before hands-on robots arrive around 2031. Somebody still has to answer a worker who was paid for the wrong number of hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my junior post could go quickly. Two months saved would cover only a little search time with a mortgage and two school-age children, and the flower stall cannot reliably replace my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd write down the mortgage and school bills and ask the lender what happens if my pay stops. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd apply for paid payroll-clerk posts only where a vacancy exists and the combined wage with the flower stall's dependable minimum covers the mortgage; if none qualify, I'd ask my cousin about a room we could rent, but I would not move the children without my partner agreeing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. The thought of a pay error is bad enough; the thought of not earning a pay slip is worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is your cousin's room available for a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin has a small spare room but has not offered it, and it would be tight for four people. I'd ask the price and whether a family could actually stay, then decide with my partner only if the mortgage became impossible to meet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about a move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children have school friends here. I would tell them we are checking our options, not that we are moving tomorrow; I do not know if a room would even be available.

say: I'd say **2028 thinking AI** reaches payroll code before 2031 robots.
I'd ask who answers workers after **wrong automated wages**.
think: I expect **my junior post** could disappear quickly.
I cannot replace my wage with **seasonal stall sales** and two months saved.
do: Ask the **mortgage lender** now about missed-wage options.
After a cut, apply for **paid payroll-clerk jobs** only if vacancies and dependable household income cover mortgage.
Ask about **cousin's room** only if no job qualifies, checking space and price; decide with partner if mortgage fails.
feel: **Alarmed** by possible wage loss and a mortgage for four.
S2.quote: The thought of a pay error is bad enough; the thought of not earning a pay slip is worse.
fieldNote: **2028 thinking AI** hits payroll coding first; 2031 robots are beside his desk-work risk.
His cousin has **not offered housing**; he would check space and price, with any move needing a joint decision if mortgage fails.

steps.text: Apply after a cut to vacant payroll-clerk posts only if household pay covers mortgage
Ask cousin whether room can house four and what it costs only if no job qualifies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years until 2031 lets us check what the software really gets right before anyone removes people from payroll. Robots arrive around 2034, but the thinking AI would reach our code and files first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might learn to audit exports if I am shown the errors slowly and on old data. Five years also gives us a chance to save more if my wage holds and the flower stall brings enough for school costs, but I cannot assume the senior developer will have time to teach me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for one afternoon a month with the senior developer to go through wrong-hour cases on copied files, if our manager frees that time. We'd save 50 monthly only when stall sales cover school costs; in the first year after 2031 I'd apply to paid payroll review posts only if those jobs exist and our dependable income covers mortgage and school bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I can work through a copied file one at a time. The date gives me time, not a guarantee that the work will be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be in the first practice file?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start with the cleaner's missing Sunday hours and make myself explain the correction before the senior shows me the answer. If I cannot explain a wrong pay slip, I am not ready to sign a payroll file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the senior developer has no time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The senior is helpful but already busy. If the manager cannot free an afternoon, I'd keep doing the Thursday exports and ask again next month.

say: I'd say **2031 thinking AI** reaches payroll code before 2034 robots.
I'd ask for **copied-file tests** before removing human payroll checks.
think: I might learn **payroll auditing** with slow, supervised practice.
I need **steady household income** before savings can grow.
do: Practice **wrong-hour cases** monthly if my manager frees senior time.
Save **50 monthly** only when stall sales cover school costs.
After 2031, apply for **paid review posts** only if vacancies and dependable income cover mortgage and school bills.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to learn from one old file at a time.
S3.quote: If I cannot explain a wrong pay slip, I am not ready to sign a payroll file.
fieldNote: **Five years** allow cautious learning through copied files, dependent on senior and manager time.
His savings and any move require **dependable household pay**, not a best-case market week.

steps.text: Practice monthly wrong-hour cases on copied files only if manager frees senior time
Save 50 monthly only if flower sales cover school costs
Apply after 2031 to paid review vacancies only if dependable income covers mortgage and school bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years until 2036 is enough time to learn the rules behind payroll instead of just pressing buttons. Thinking AI still reaches code before 2039 robots, so the extra years should be used while wages are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might have a human review role, or I might still be junior and waiting for a cut. Our mortgage and the market stall's uneven weeks are current, though my developer wage covers the basic payment; I can't call the household fully secure just because 2036 sounds far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking Thursday exports and add to my notebook of wrong-hour cases. If stall sales cover school costs, we'd save 50 monthly and review the mortgage balance each year; in the first year after 2036 I'd switch to a paid payroll review role only if a signed offer plus dependable stall income covers the mortgage and school bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A decade gives me room to learn, but I would still be checking the market takings and the mortgage statement this month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you keep in the notebook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The notebook would show the missing Sunday hours and how we corrected the rule, without worker names. I can show payroll reasoning at an interview without taking anyone's pay details.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the car soon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I will keep the older car while it runs. We would rather make the mortgage payment than borrow for a nicer car on an uncertain future wage.

say: I'd say **2036 thinking AI** reaches payroll code before 2039 robots.
I'd use the decade to learn **payroll rules** while wages still come in.
think: I might find **human review work** by 53, but I cannot assume it.
I still face **uneven stall sales** and monthly mortgage payments.
do: Keep **Thursday exports** and a notebook of wrong-hour cases.
Save **50 monthly** if stall sales cover school costs, reviewing mortgage yearly.
After 2036, switch only for a **signed review offer** covering mortgage and school bills with dependable stall income.
feel: **Uneasy** about current household money, with time to learn.
S4.quote: I can show payroll reasoning at an interview without taking anyone's pay details.
fieldNote: **Current mortgage pressure** and seasonal sales make a distant AI date uneasy rather than automatically calm.
He keeps **manual payroll skill** visible, saves conditionally and requires a signed wage-covering offer before moving.

steps.text: Keep checking Thursday payroll exports and recording wrong-hour cases without names
Save 50 monthly if stall sales cover school costs and review mortgage yearly
Switch after 2036 only for signed payroll review offer covering mortgage and school bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because payroll code is almost all thinking work, and I could be the junior let go. A clear notice period, mortgage breathing room and paid review vacancies with a wage we can actually live on would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what happens to a worker when a pay slip is wrong. The cleaner whose Sunday hours vanished had to wait for a correction; that is a real person, not a line in my test file.

headlineQuote: The cleaner whose Sunday hours vanished had to wait for a correction; that is a real person, not a line in my test file.
portrait: Marco, **43**, is a junior payroll-software developer with a two-year diploma and a habit of checking exports against paper rotas.
His **typical pay** covers the mortgage, while seasonal flower-stall sales help with two children's school costs; he has two months saved.
He avoids AI tools, but would inspect **copied files** with a colleague after the firm proves a process catches missing hours.
Steady disruption makes him **anxious** about his junior seat; fast 2028 AGI alarms him despite some nearby software firms.
With more time, he pursues **supervised audit practice**, conditional saving and paid review work only at a wage covering family bills.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his payroll coding wage before his two-month cushion supports a search.
whatWouldHelp: A **clear notice period**, mortgage relief and genuinely paid review vacancies would help him respond.
